title: The one sent away (6.15)
hook: the mother of his son is sent back to Africa and his heart is torn; a painful passage
tomorrow: how big is God, if he isn't a body?

segments.voice: Two weeks into the Confessions. This week: half of my soul, love them in God, charming, but, the bishop received me, reading in silence. And yesterday, a promise undone by the roar of a crowd.

A gentle warning: this is a painful passage, and the Confessions doesn't hide it. Some families have a person who isn't in the photos anymore, and nobody says why. Augustine's book has one. He is engaged to be married, to a girl still too young to marry. And the woman he has lived with, the mother of his son, is torn from his side as an obstacle to the marriage. Who does the book send away? Her. And it never gives her name.
screen: `A PAINFUL PASSAGE.` → `THE ONE NOT IN THE PHOTOS.` → `SENT AWAY, NEVER NAMED.`

segments.voice: Augustine writes his own side first. His heart, which clung to her, was torn and wounded and bleeding. Then he gives her a single sentence. She went back to Africa, vowing to God never to know another man, and leaving their son with him. That's all the text gives her. Some readers stop right there and say it plainly: she was wronged. She loses her home, her partner and her child, and makes a vow of her own, while he, as he admits, couldn't wait for the wedding and took another woman. Augustine doesn't defend himself. He calls himself a slave of lust, not a lover of marriage, and says the wound didn't heal; it festered. The book is his account, told against himself. Hers we never hear. What it does allow is a way to read it: name the wrong without looking away, and remember her vow, made to God by a woman the story never names.
screen: `TORN, WOUNDED, BLEEDING.` · `ONE SENTENCE FOR HER.` · `A VOW OF HER OWN.` · `TOLD AGAINST HIMSELF.` · then, large: `SHE WAS WRONGED.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and hold in mind the woman this passage never names, and with her, anyone you know of who was set aside to suit someone else's plans. Keep them company in your thoughts for the length of the sit. Catholics who pray can pray for them, by name or with no name at all.
The one sent away. In book six, the mother of Augustine's son is sent back to Africa; she makes a vow to God, and the book never gives her name.
Your line: she was wronged, and one sentence is enough to remember her by. Two weeks, done.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for those who have been wronged and for those who wronged them; the Church teaches the equal dignity of every person. Readers of the Confessions often discuss this passage openly as a hard part of Augustine's story.

notes: For parents: a painful passage about a woman sent away from her partner and child; the hook opens with a gentle warning, and nothing sexual is described beyond Augustine's own words 'slave of lust'.

Sensitive passage, per the outline. Confessions 6.15 paraphrased: she was torn from his side as a hindrance to the marriage; his heart clave to her and was torn, wounded, bleeding; she returned to Africa vowing never to know another man, leaving their son with him; he could not wait for the bride and took another woman, 'no lover of wedlock, but a slave of lust'; the wound did not heal but festered. Confirm.

Confessions 6.13 paraphrased: he was betrothed to a girl under the age for marriage (the text gives the gap in years; the voice gives no number). The text does not say who sent her away; the voice keeps the passive voice ('is torn from his side'). Confirm.
'She was wronged' is the index carry; the voice attributes the judgment to 'some readers' and to Augustine's own self-accusation. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this framing.
The woman is unnamed in the Confessions; their son (named elsewhere in the book) is not named here, to stay with 6.15.
